newsitem.title: FRANCE: French bishops lash out at liberal economy.
newsitem.headline: French bishops lash out at liberal economy.

text.p: France's Roman Catholic bishops lashed out on Thursday at the modern liberal economy for widening the wealth gap and leaving behind the weak who could not keep pace.

Stepping into a debate raging in a country worried by record unemployment, economic stagnation and corruption scandals, the Bishops' Conference said growing numbers were unable to keep up with rapid changes, and an unbearable gap was widening between those who strived and those who were crushed.
While the ranks of the poor were swelling, too much money was flowing around and where it was going was unclear.
"Too much money makes no human sense," the bishops said in a statement.
"Progress will not be possible until the central issue has been resolved: that of the sharing out of revenue."

Record unemployment in France has swelled the ranks of the homeless and destitute while confidence in politicians and businesmen has been shaken by failure to revive the economy and by a series of corruption scandals in the 1980s that are now coming to light.
The bishops accused economists and politicians of short-sightedness.
"A pragmatism limited to the immediate future is ruling. It mistakes for realism a law of the market obsessed with short-term profitability and often deprived of morality," they said.

"Finance in the end turns against the economy. Politics, so necessary to a nation, deal from day to day with increasingly complex sets of rules. Administrative power cannot replace political responsibility to give a new breath and hope."
The bishops said a society made fragile by its divisions could fall prey to demagogues and violent ideologies.
"Social divisions weaken resistance to the unacceptable. What undermines the dignity of man is unacceptable," they said.

All mainstream French political parties have voiced concern over the rise of the far-right, anti-immigrant National Front which advocates sending all immigrants home and won 15 percent of the votes in last year's presidential election.
